# Bundle composition

`scripts/bundle-size.mjs` already answers *how much* ships: it sums the client
JS and CSS in `.next/static` and fails a build that grows the gzip total by more
than 5% and 10 KB against the latest `main` baseline.

That is enough to catch a regression but not to explain one. When the number
moves, the first question is always "which package?", and answering it meant
building locally and reading chunk filenames. This document and the
`composition` command answer it from CI instead (#266).

## Using it

```sh
npm run build            # without ANALYZE_BUNDLE, composition is unavailable
ANALYZE_BUNDLE=1 npm run build
node scripts/bundle-size.mjs measure      # writes bundle-composition-current.json
node scripts/bundle-size.mjs report       # size + composition, as the CI summary
node scripts/bundle-size.mjs composition  # composition only
```

`report` is what CI runs, and it now emits a composition table underneath the
size table, with a per-package "change vs `main`" column. The largest increases
are called out separately, which is usually the whole answer.

The CI job builds with `ANALYZE_BUNDLE=1`, caches the composition baseline from
`main` the same way it already did for the size baseline, and uploads
`bundle-composition-current.json` as an artifact on every run so a reviewer can
diff composition without rebuilding.

## How the attribution works

Turbopack's minified client chunks name no modules, so bytes cannot be traced
back to their origin from the chunk text. `ANALYZE_BUNDLE=1` makes
`next.config.ts` set `productionBrowserSourceMaps`, which makes Turbopack emit a
source map per chunk. `scripts/bundle-composition.mjs` then:

1. Resolves each chunk's map through its `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment. This
   matters: Turbopack names a map independently of its chunk
   (`03zi82on67aet.js` -> `31eed2o9wbwkr.js.map`), so assuming an adjacent
   `.map` finds nothing.
2. Decodes the map's base64-VLQ `mappings` and charges each generated byte
   range to the source its segment names, with source-less segments inheriting
   the previous one.
3. Rolls the sources up to the owning package, first-party code, or the
   unmapped bucket.

Source maps are opt-in rather than always on because they roughly double build
output and add time, and only the bundle job needs them.

Two honest limits:

- Attribution is per source map, not per byte-exact AST, so treat it as a strong
  signal rather than an accounting. A segment owns everything up to the next
  segment's column, ignoring column-level mappings inside that span.
- Turbopack maps no CSS chunk and one large runtime chunk, listed under
  "Files Turbopack does not map" below.

The decoder and attribution are covered by `test/bundle-composition.test.ts`,
including a check that every byte of a file is accounted for.

## Tree-shaking and duplicates

`@stellar/stellar-sdk` is the dependency whose shipped size depends most on
import shape, so it gets its own section in the report: total, share, and the
SDK modules responsible, largest first. A jump in
`src/base/generated/curr_generated.js` in particular means an XDR-typed import
crept in and pulled the whole currency table along.

Duplicate versions are read from `package-lock.json`, so a duplicate is caught
even if it happens to be fully tree-shaken away. The report only lists
duplicates that actually reach the browser, because a lockfile is full of
build-tool duplicates that never ship and listing them all buries the signal.

## Snapshot

Recorded from a production build on 2026-09-27.

| Metric | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Static assets measured | 38 |
| Total shipped | 1549.1 KB raw / 450.5 KB gzip |
| Attributed via source maps | 1543.0 KB across 63 buckets |

### The Stellar SDK

`@stellar/stellar-sdk` is the largest dependency at **276.2 KB (17.9%)**, so it is worth knowing which parts of it actually ship:

| SDK module | Bytes |
| --- | --- |
| `src/base/generated/curr_generated.js` | 99.1 KB |
| `src/contract/spec.ts` | 18.9 KB |
| `src/base/transaction_builder.ts` | 14.0 KB |
| `src/rpc/server.ts` | 12.4 KB |
| `src/contract/assembled_transaction.ts` | 10.0 KB |
| `src/bindings/sac-spec.ts` | 9.6 KB |

`src/base/generated/curr_generated.js` is the bulk of it: the XDR currency table, which anything touching XDR types pulls in wholesale. Treat it as a floor rather than a regression — the rest of the SDK's footprint tracks which contract and RPC helpers get imported, and a new import of a helper that reaches an XDR type will show up here as a jump in this file.

### Dependencies shipped at more than one version

None. Every dependency that reaches the browser resolves to exactly one version, so nothing is duplicated in the client bundle.

The lockfile does contain 46 packages at more than one version, but all of them are build- or dev-only (eslint and its dependencies, the lightningcss platform binaries, glob and friends). The report separates the two so the lockfile's noise does not read as a bundle problem.

### Files Turbopack does not map

`productionBrowserSourceMaps` produces no map for these, so their bytes land in the `(unmapped files)` bucket instead of being attributed:

- `chunks/0cz1d0mv5g_q7.js` (110.0 KB)
- `chunks/0y4d3x61-2xj2.css` (85.5 KB)
- `z8ZLnAeyzbGQjyPPPwKry/_buildManifest.js` (0.2 KB)
- `z8ZLnAeyzbGQjyPPPwKry/_clientMiddlewareManifest.js` (0.5 KB)
- `z8ZLnAeyzbGQjyPPPwKry/_ssgManifest.js` (0.1 KB)

That is 12.7% of attributed bytes: a 110 KB framework/polyfill chunk and the compiled stylesheet. If that share moves substantially, treat the per-package numbers as proportions of the mapped remainder rather than of the whole bundle.
